subject: PE
overview: Plan about 30 minutes per lesson: a 5-minute dynamic warm-up, one skill taught with 2–3 short cues, drill practice, a game or challenge, and a cool-down with one check question. Fifth grade is a FITNESSGRAM year: baseline tests in week 4 and post-tests in week 35 — compare your child only with their own earlier scores and the Healthy Fitness Zone, never with siblings or friends. Model each skill yourself (or show a short video), give one specific piece of feedback at a time, and praise effort, safety and sportsmanship as much as success.

weeks.prep: Gather cones, a timer and a water bottle; mark a play area about 15 × 15 m. Write the five fitness components on index cards with their definitions on separate cards for matching. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Thinking stretching means holding a stretch before exercise. Before activity use moving (dynamic) stretches; save held (static) stretches for the cool-down when muscles are warm.
Confusing muscular strength with muscular endurance. Strength is how much force a muscle can exert once (a heavy lift); endurance is how many times or how long it can keep working (many curl-ups).

days.guide: Demonstrate each warm-up move for about 30 seconds (high knees, butt kicks, arm circles, walking lunges, skips) with one cue each, e.g. 'knees up to hip height.' Your child copies, then play 5 minutes of tag.

questions.q: Why do we warm up before exercise?
questions.a: To raise heart rate and muscle temperature and loosen joints so the body is ready to work and less likely to be injured.

days.guide: Set up four stations (jog in place, push-ups, plank, sit-and-reach stretch), 1 minute each. Afterwards your child matches each component card to its definition and names the station that trained it.

questions.q: Which station trained aerobic capacity, and what does that term mean?
questions.a: The jog — aerobic capacity is how well the heart and lungs deliver oxygen to working muscles over a long time.

questions.q: What is body composition?
questions.a: The proportion of fat to lean tissue (muscle, bone, organs) in the body.

days.guide: Walk the space together and point out hazards (sprinklers, curbs, rocks); set boundary cones. Review rules: stay in bounds, look up, call 'stop' if someone gets hurt. Play Sharks and Minnows, coaching your child to move into open space.

questions.q: Name two things you check before playing in a space.
questions.a: Any two: hazards on the ground (holes, rocks, glass), clear boundaries away from streets or walls, enough room between players, water and shade available.

days.guide: Jog-walk for 10 minutes, then lead a 5-minute static cool-down: hamstrings, quadriceps, calves, chest/shoulders, hip flexors, holding each 15–30 seconds without bouncing.

questions.q: How long should you hold a cool-down stretch, and should you bounce?
questions.a: About 15–30 seconds, gently to mild tension, with no bouncing.

days.guide: Your child leads you (or a sibling) through the warm-up, giving each move's cue. Then ask them to name and define all five components.

questions.q: Name the five components of health-related fitness.
questions.a: Aerobic capacity, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, and body composition.

weeks.assessment_key: Warm-up (4 = leads all five moves in order with clear cues and correct form; 3 = one move or cue missing; 2 = needs several prompts; 1 = cannot lead). Oral check: aerobic capacity = heart/lungs supplying oxygen over time; muscular strength = maximum force at one time; muscular endurance = working many times without tiring; flexibility = range of motion at a joint; body composition = ratio of fat to lean mass. Proficient = all five named and four or more defined correctly.

weeks.prep: Gather a stopwatch, two cones 20 m apart, and a FITNESSGRAM PACER audio track (free versions are online). Measure a quarter mile (e.g., one lap of a school track, or map a route). Prepare a simple graph with walk/jog/sprint on the x-axis. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Using the thumb to take a pulse. The thumb has its own pulse; use the index and middle fingers lightly on the wrist (thumb side) or neck.
Starting the PACER too fast. The early levels are slow on purpose — jogging at the beep, not sprinting, saves energy for later levels.

days.guide: Show your child how to find the radial pulse (thumb side of the wrist) and carotid pulse (side of the neck beside the windpipe). Sitting quietly, count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4.

questions.q: You count 21 beats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate?
questions.a: 84 beats per minute (21 × 4).

days.guide: Walk 1 minute and take pulse; rest until close to resting; jog 1 minute and take pulse; rest; sprint 1 minute (or 30 seconds) and take pulse. Your child graphs the three numbers.

questions.q: Predict which activity gives the highest heart rate and explain why.
questions.a: Sprinting — working muscles need much more oxygen, so the heart beats faster to pump more blood.

days.guide: Explain the PACER: run 20 m before each beep, which gets faster each level. Practice for 10 minutes, coaching 'arrive with the beep, turn, go' rather than racing ahead.

questions.q: What is the best pacing strategy on the PACER?
questions.a: Run just fast enough to reach the line as the beep sounds; don't sprint early levels, so you save energy for the faster ones.

days.guide: Time each of four quarter-mile jog-walks and write the times down. Coach your child to keep each lap within about 15 seconds of the first.

questions.q: Your lap times were 2:30, 2:40, 3:20, 3:45. What does that show about your pacing?
questions.a: The pace was not even — you started too fast and slowed a lot. Start slower so later laps stay close to the first.

days.guide: Your child explains to you, using their graph, why heart rate rises with exercise, then records today's resting and post-exercise rates on a chart.

questions.q: Why does heart rate go up when you exercise?
questions.a: Muscles working harder need more oxygen and fuel, so the heart beats faster to pump more oxygen-rich blood to them.

weeks.assessment_key: Heart rate graph: correctly labeled axes; three bars or points with walk < jog < sprint; resting rate typically about 60–100 bpm. Explanation (proficient): 'Exercise makes muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster to deliver it; harder exercise = higher heart rate.' Rubric 4 = accurate graph plus explanation with oxygen/muscle link; 3 = graph plus general explanation; 2 = incomplete graph or vague explanation; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Cut a cardboard curl-up strip 4.5 inches wide (FITNESSGRAM size for ages 10+). Gather a mat or towel, a ruler/yardstick, and a box with a ruler on top for sit-and-reach. Print or write a form checklist for each test. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Pulling on the neck during curl-ups. Arms stay straight at the sides with palms sliding along the mat; the head comes up because the stomach muscles curl the shoulders.
Arching the back too high in the trunk lift. Lift slowly to no more than 12 inches; higher is not better and can strain the back.
Sagging hips in push-ups. Keep a straight line from head to heels like a plank.

days.guide: Model the curl-up: knees bent, feet flat, arms straight with fingertips at the strip's near edge, curl until fingertips reach the far edge, then back so the head touches the mat. Use the cadence of one curl-up every 3 seconds; do 3 sets of 10.

questions.q: How far do your fingertips slide on each curl-up?
questions.a: Across the 4.5-inch strip, from the near edge to the far edge.

days.guide: Model the 90-degree push-up: hands under shoulders, body straight, lower until elbows bend to 90 degrees, push up. Practice wall and knee push-ups if needed, then try full ones at a 3-second cadence.

questions.q: How low do you go in the FITNESSGRAM push-up?
questions.a: Until the elbows bend to a 90-degree angle (upper arms parallel to the floor), keeping the body straight.

days.guide: Trunk lift: face down, hands under thighs, slowly lift the upper body up to 12 inches and hold while you measure chin-to-floor. Sit-and-reach: one leg straight, the other knee bent, reach forward four times and hold the fourth. Measure each side.

questions.q: What is the maximum score counted for the trunk lift, and why?
questions.a: 12 inches — lifting higher than that is not needed and could strain the lower back.

days.guide: Run a 6-station circuit (squats, plank, curl-ups, push-ups, wall sit, lunges), 30 seconds each with 15 seconds rest. Watch form, not speed.

questions.q: Which two stations mostly build core endurance?
questions.a: Plank and curl-ups.

days.guide: Your child watches you perform each test and marks the form checklist, then tells you one thing done well and one fix.

questions.q: During a push-up, my hips sag toward the floor. What feedback do you give?
questions.a: Tighten your stomach and keep a straight line from head to heels.

weeks.assessment_key: Form checklist (one point per cue): Curl-up — knees bent ~140°, feet flat, arms straight, fingers slide across strip, head returns to mat, 3-second cadence. Push-up — hands under shoulders, straight body, elbows to 90°, full extension, cadence. Trunk lift — slow lift, eyes on a spot on the floor, ≤12 in, no bouncing. Sit-and-reach — one knee bent, straight leg flat, hands stacked, four reaches, hold the last. Proficient = performs and identifies at least 80% of cues.

weeks.prep: Print a FITNESSGRAM Healthy Fitness Zone (HFZ) chart for your child's age and sex (available from FITNESSGRAM/the California Department of Education), a score sheet, the PACER audio, stopwatch and the curl-up strip. Test on rested days with water nearby; space tests across the week. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Thinking the goal is to beat other kids. FITNESSGRAM compares you to a health standard (the Healthy Fitness Zone), not to other people.
Believing one low score means 'unfit.' A baseline just shows where you start; scores rise with training.

days.guide: Warm up, then run the PACER until your child misses the line twice (or run/walk one mile and time it). Record laps or time immediately.

questions.q: When does the PACER end for a runner?
questions.a: The second time they fail to reach the line before the beep.

days.guide: Curl-up test at 1 every 3 seconds until two form errors or 75 reached; rest; then the push-up test at the same cadence until two form errors. Record both.

questions.q: What is the cadence for the curl-up and push-up tests?
questions.a: One repetition every 3 seconds.

days.guide: Trunk lift: two trials, record the best (max 12 in). Back-saver sit-and-reach: measure each side to the nearest half inch (max 12 in).

questions.q: Why do we measure the sit-and-reach on both sides?
questions.a: Flexibility can differ between the right and left legs, so each side is tested separately.

days.guide: Look up each score on the HFZ chart together. Your child highlights scores in the HFZ green and circles any 'Needs Improvement.'

questions.q: If your score is in the Healthy Fitness Zone, what does that mean?
questions.a: Your fitness in that area meets the level associated with good health for your age and sex.

days.guide: Your child writes one goal ('I will increase my PACER from 18 to 25 laps by May') plus an activity to reach it. Finish with an active game of their choice.

questions.q: Make this goal specific: 'Get better at push-ups.'
questions.a: Example: 'I will go from 6 to 10 push-ups by the spring test by doing push-ups 3 days a week.'

weeks.assessment_key: Score sheet complete for all five items (PACER laps or mile time, curl-ups, push-ups, trunk lift inches, sit-and-reach L/R inches), each compared correctly to the HFZ chart. Goal statement rubric: 4 = specific number, deadline, and a matching activity with frequency; 3 = specific and measurable but no plan; 2 = vague goal; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Size each rope: standing on the middle, handles should reach the armpits. Choose music with a clear, steady beat (about 120 beats per minute). Jump on a smooth, non-slip surface. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Jumping too high. Jump only an inch or two off the ground, landing softly on the balls of the feet.
Turning the rope with whole arms. Keep elbows close to the sides and turn with the wrists.

days.guide: Check rope size. Model the basic bounce (both feet, small jumps) and alternate step (like jogging in place). Practice 3 × 1-minute sets with rests.

questions.q: How do you know a rope is the right length?
questions.a: Standing on the middle with both feet, the handles reach about the armpits.

days.guide: Teach skier (jump side to side), bell (jump forward and back) and side-straddle (feet apart, together). Each 20 times; say the name aloud as you jump.

questions.q: Describe the bell trick.
questions.a: Feet together, jumping forward and backward like a bell swinging.

days.guide: Play the song and jump, switching trick every 8 counts. Count aloud '1–8' with your child at first.

questions.q: Why count in 8s when jumping to music?
questions.a: Most popular music is grouped in phrases of 8 beats, so changing every 8 counts keeps you on the beat.

days.guide: Take resting pulse, jump for 2 minutes continuously, take pulse. Compare to the jogging number from week 2.

questions.q: Was jump rope more or less intense than jogging for you? How do you know?
questions.a: Answer depends on the data — the activity with the higher heart rate afterward was more intense (jump rope is often as high or higher).

days.guide: Your child performs a 30-second trick sequence, then you count successful jumps in 1 minute of basic bounce.

questions.q: What two cues help you jump longer without missing?
questions.a: Small low jumps on the balls of the feet, and turning with the wrists with elbows in.

weeks.assessment_key: Trick checklist (✓ = 5 in a row without a miss): basic bounce, alternate step, skier, bell, side-straddle. 1-minute count recorded (typical 5th-grade range is roughly 60–120; compare with your child's later scores). Proficient = all five tricks checked and a steady rhythm.

weeks.prep: Gather individual ropes plus a long rope (about 4–5 m; or tie two ropes together). If you lack a second turner, tie one end to a fence or tree at waist height. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Crossing the arms at the elbows only for criss-cross. Cross deeply so the hands reach the opposite hips, making a big loop.
Running straight at the long rope. Enter from the side at an angle, right after the rope passes the top and hits the ground.

days.guide: Model criss-cross: on the downswing, cross arms to opposite hips, jump through, then open. Teach the side swing (rope swings beside the body with hands together) followed by opening into a jump.

questions.q: Where should your hands go in a criss-cross?
questions.a: Cross deeply so each hand is near the opposite hip.

days.guide: Practice 'power jumps' (high, tight jumps) with fast wrist turns. Try one double under after several singles; celebrate attempts.

questions.q: What two things make a double under possible?
questions.a: Jumping a bit higher and turning the rope much faster with the wrists, so it passes under twice in one jump.

days.guide: With two turners, practice: stand near a turner, wait for the rope to hit the ground and go up, run in to the middle, jump 10, and run out the side diagonally.

questions.q: When is the right moment to enter a long rope?
questions.a: Right after the rope hits the ground and starts moving away/up ('front door' entry).

days.guide: Your child picks one trick and coaches you using two cues and encouragement ('Elbows in! Great rhythm!').

questions.q: Give one cue and one encouraging comment for the skier.
questions.a: Cue: 'Keep feet together and jump side to side over a line.' Encouragement: 'Nice steady rhythm—keep going!'

days.guide: Your child performs five different tricks; mark mastered (5 in a row) or developing on a chart.

questions.q: Which trick was hardest, and what will you practice?
questions.a: Answer varies; a strong answer names the trick and a specific cue to practice (e.g., 'criss-cross—cross deeper').

weeks.assessment_key: Trick mastery chart: list ≥5 tricks (e.g., basic, skier, bell, criss-cross, side swing, long-rope entry). Mastered = 5 consecutive successful jumps. 4 = 5+ tricks mastered; 3 = 4 mastered; 2 = 2–3; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: Gather music at several tempos, cones, and lummi sticks (or two wooden spoons/paper towel tubes per person). Learn one simple lummi pattern ahead of time (tap floor, tap together, tap partner's sticks). Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Mixing up a gallop and a slide. A gallop goes forward with the same lead foot; a slide goes sideways.
Rushing the beat. Clap the beat first, then move, so steps land on the beat.

days.guide: Call out skip, slide, gallop, leap and hop while music plays; change the tempo and have your child match it.

questions.q: What is the difference between a hop and a jump?
questions.a: A hop takes off and lands on the same one foot; a jump lands on two feet (or takes off from two).

days.guide: Sit facing each other. Teach a 4-count lummi pattern: tap ends on floor (1), tap sticks together (2), tap partner's right stick (3), tap together (4). Repeat to 4/4 music.

questions.q: How many beats are in each measure of 4/4 time?
questions.a: Four beats.

days.guide: Build four 8-count sequences (e.g., 8 skips, 8 slides right, 4 hops + 4 jumps, 8 gallops) and string them together.

questions.q: How many counts are in four 8-count sequences?
questions.a: 32 counts.

days.guide: Your child designs a 32-count routine mixing locomotor moves and jump-rope tricks and writes it down by counts.

questions.q: Your routine has 8 skier jumps, 8 skips and 8 slides. How many more counts do you need for 32?
questions.a: 8 more counts.

days.guide: Your child performs the routine to music, then explains where the moves change. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: How did your routine follow the beat?
questions.a: Each move lasted a set number of counts (8) and changes happened at the start of a new 8-count phrase on the beat.

weeks.assessment_key: Rhythmic routine (4 = 32 counts, at least 4 different moves, stays on beat throughout, smooth changes on count 1; 3 = minor beat slips; 2 = loses the beat often or fewer moves; 1 = incomplete). Child explains that changes happen at the start of 8-count phrases.

weeks.prep: Gather ropes, music, and a phone/tablet to record. Optional: look up 'Jump Rope for Heart' (American Heart Association) for ideas. Invite an audience for Friday. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Thinking a routine is just a list of tricks. Transitions (how you move from one trick to the next without stopping) are part of the routine.
Giving only general feedback ('good job'). Feedback should name a specific cue: 'Your criss-cross was on beat; open the arms sooner.'

days.guide: Help your child write a 1-minute routine with at least 6 tricks and how they'll transition (e.g., 8 bounces → 8 skiers).

questions.q: About how many 8-counts fill 1 minute of music at 120 beats per minute?
questions.a: 120 beats ÷ 8 = 15 eight-counts.

days.guide: Practice the routine with music three times, counting aloud at first, then silently. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What should you do if you miss a jump in the middle?
questions.a: Restart the rope quickly and rejoin on the next 8-count without stopping the routine.

days.guide: Record the routine and watch together. Your child names two specific spots to improve. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Give an example of a specific improvement note.
questions.a: e.g., 'At count 33 I stopped to switch to skier—add a bounce step to transition smoothly.'

days.guide: Family jump-a-thon: everyone jumps in 1–2 minute turns; total the minutes. Talk about how jumping is good for heart health.

questions.q: Why is jumping rope good for the heart?
questions.a: It is vigorous aerobic exercise that makes the heart and lungs work harder, which strengthens them over time.

days.guide: Your child performs for an audience, then watches another performer and gives one praise and one cue-based suggestion.

questions.q: What makes feedback helpful?
questions.a: It is specific, uses a skill cue, is kind, and gives one thing to try next.

weeks.assessment_key: Routine rubric (each 1–4): Tricks — 6+ different tricks performed correctly; Rhythm — on the beat throughout; Transitions — no stops between tricks; Feedback — gives specific, cue-based, kind feedback. Proficient = 3 or higher in each.

weeks.prep: Gather a size-4 soccer ball and 6–10 cones. Set a cone line with cones about 1 m apart, a figure-8 with two cones 5 m apart, and a 20 m straight. Your child should wear sneakers or cleats. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Kicking the ball far ahead while dribbling in tight spaces. Use small, soft touches so the ball stays within one step.
Looking only at the ball. Glance up between touches to see space and defenders.

days.guide: Model small touches with the inside and outside of both feet through the cone line. Your child goes through 6 times, alternating feet.

questions.q: Why use small touches when dribbling in traffic?
questions.a: Keeping the ball close gives you control and makes it harder for a defender to take.

days.guide: Teach an inside cut (pull the ball across your body with the inside of the foot) and outside cut (push away with the outside). Practice around cones and in a figure 8.

questions.q: Which part of the foot do you use to cut the ball away from your body?
questions.a: The outside of the foot.

days.guide: Dribble 20 m at speed with longer pushes, then stop the ball with the sole. Repeat 6 times.

questions.q: How is a speed dribble different from close control?
questions.a: Longer touches pushed into open space ahead so you can run faster; fewer touches.

days.guide: Play dribble tag: everyone dribbles in a small square; the tagger tries to tag players while keeping their own ball. Tagged players do 5 toe taps and rejoin.

questions.q: How do you keep control while escaping a tagger?
questions.a: Keep the ball close, use cuts to change direction, and keep your head up to find open space.

days.guide: Time your child through a cone course twice and note control (ball touches each cone? lost ball?).

questions.q: Which matters more in the course: speed or control? Why?
questions.a: Control first — losing the ball costs more time than dribbling a little slower.

weeks.assessment_key: Cone course: record two times. Control checklist: uses both feet, small touches near cones, inside and outside cuts, head up at least sometimes, stops with sole at the end. Proficient = 4 of 5 cues and second time equal or faster with no lost balls.

weeks.prep: Gather a ball, a wall or rebounder, and cones for 3–4 gates (two cones about 1 m apart). Review cues: plant foot beside the ball, toe up, ankle locked, strike with inside of foot, follow through to target. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Toe-kicking passes. Use the inside of the foot with the toe up and ankle locked for accuracy.
Stopping the ball dead and then looking. A good first touch pushes the ball slightly into space ready for the next move.

days.guide: Model the push pass: plant foot beside the ball pointing at the target, toe up, ankle locked, strike with the inside of the foot. Your child does 50 passes against a wall alternating feet.

questions.q: Where should your plant foot point?
questions.a: At the target, beside the ball.

days.guide: Toss or roll passes; your child traps with the sole, then the inside of the foot (cushion by pulling back slightly), then the thigh, and passes back.

questions.q: How do you 'cushion' a trap?
questions.a: Relax and give with the ball, pulling the foot or thigh back slightly as it arrives so it doesn't bounce away.

days.guide: Set gates; your child passes through gates to you; score one point per successful gate pass in 2 minutes.

questions.q: Why does following through toward the target matter?
questions.a: It sends the ball in the direction your foot finishes, improving accuracy.

days.guide: Have your child jog across the yard; pass ahead of them so they receive without stopping. Then switch roles.

questions.q: Where should you aim a lead pass?
questions.a: In front of the moving teammate, into the space they are running to.

days.guide: Your child watches you pass and fills a feedback form using the cues: plant foot, ankle locked, follow-through.

questions.q: My pass went to the left of you. What might have caused it?
questions.a: The plant foot or follow-through pointed left, or the ball was struck off-center.

weeks.assessment_key: Passing gates: record points in 2 minutes (compare with later tries). Peer feedback form proficient if it correctly checks plant foot, locked ankle, inside-foot contact and follow-through, and gives one specific fix.

weeks.prep: Gather a ball, a goal (or two cones 4 m apart), targets for the corners (cones or buckets), and a tape measure. Gloves optional for goalkeeping; use gentle shots. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Shooting with the toe. Strike with the laces (instep) with the toe pointed down for power and control.
Leaning back when shooting. Leaning back sends the ball high; keep the chest over the ball.

days.guide: Model the instep drive: approach at a slight angle, plant foot beside the ball, toe pointed down, strike with the laces, follow through. Shoot from 10 m aiming at corners.

questions.q: What part of the foot strikes the ball in an instep drive?
questions.a: The laces (top of the foot), toe pointed down.

days.guide: Teach the punt: hold ball out, drop it, kick with laces before it bounces. Measure the best of 5.

questions.q: Why must the toe be pointed when punting?
questions.a: So the hard, flat laces make contact and the ball goes up and far instead of off to the side.

days.guide: Teach the W catch (thumbs and index fingers form a W behind the ball for chest-high or higher shots) and the scoop (low ball: bend, hands behind it, scoop to the chest). Shoot gently at your child.

questions.q: When do you use a W catch versus a scoop?
questions.a: W catch for balls at chest height or higher; scoop for low or rolling balls.

days.guide: Play 1-v-1: one shoots from 10 m, one keeps goal; switch every 3 shots. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Where is the hardest place for a keeper to save?
questions.a: Low in the corners, far from the keeper's hands.

days.guide: Your child shoots 10 times at labeled zones (corners and middle) and records hits. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: If 6 of 10 shots hit the target, what is your accuracy?

weeks.assessment_key: Shooting accuracy record: zones hit out of 10 with percentage calculated correctly. Form cues: plant foot beside the ball, laces contact, toe down, follow-through toward the target. Proficient = 50% or higher and 3 of 4 cues.

weeks.prep: Gather a ball, cones for a small field (about 20 × 15 m) and goals, and different-colored shirts. Invite siblings, neighbors or co-op friends for 2-v-2 or 3-v-3 if possible. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Everyone chasing the ball ('beehive soccer'). On offense, spread out to open space; on defense, mark a player.
Defending by rushing in. Stay goal-side (between the attacker and your goal) and wait for a chance to take the ball.

days.guide: Play 2-v-1 keep-away (you as the defender). Pause and ask where the open space is. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Where should the player without the ball move?
questions.a: To open space where there is a clear passing line, away from the defender.

days.guide: Your child defends you 1-v-1, staying goal-side, knees bent, side-on, and not diving in. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What does 'goal-side' mean?
questions.a: Positioned between the attacker and the goal you're defending.

days.guide: Play a small-sided game. Pause once each half to ask where teammates should be. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Name one offensive and one defensive strategy you used.
questions.a: Offense: spread out/move to open space/support the ball carrier. Defense: mark a player/stay goal-side/close passing lanes.

days.guide: Play with players calling their own fouls and out-of-bounds; any disagreement is settled quickly by rock-paper-scissors.

questions.q: Why is self-officiating a test of sportsmanship?
questions.a: Players must be honest and fair even when it costs their team, and solve disputes calmly.

days.guide: Play a game while you mark the skill and strategy checklist; afterwards your child writes 3–4 sentences on their sportsmanship.

questions.q: Give an example of good sportsmanship in soccer.
questions.a: Helping up a fallen opponent, admitting a ball went out off you, shaking hands, or encouraging teammates.

weeks.assessment_key: Game-play checklist (✓ observed): dribbles with control, passes to an open teammate, moves to space without the ball, stays goal-side on defense, shoots when open, follows rules/calls honestly. Proficient = 4 of 6. Reflection rubric: 4 = specific examples of fair play and a goal for improvement; 3 = specific example; 2 = general statement; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Gather tennis balls, a hula hoop or chalk targets on a wall, and a tape measure. Mark throw lines at 5, 10 and 15 m. Use a slow-motion phone camera for Thursday. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Stepping with the same foot as the throwing arm. Step toward the target with the opposite foot (opposition).
Throwing with just the arm. Power comes from rotating the hips and trunk, then the arm whips through.

days.guide: Teach the cues: side to target, arm back, step with opposite foot, rotate hips, follow through across the body. Throw 20 at a wall target.

questions.q: A right-handed thrower steps with which foot?
questions.a: The left foot (opposite foot).

days.guide: Throw for distance at a low (flat), medium (about 45°), and high (straight up-ish) release; measure each. Your child decides which is best.

questions.q: Which release angle usually gives the most distance?
questions.a: A medium angle, around 35–45 degrees; too flat hits the ground early, too high goes up instead of out.

days.guide: Throw 5 at the target from 5, 10 and 15 m; record hits at each distance. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What should you change when the target is farther away?
questions.a: Use more force (bigger step and hip rotation) and a slightly higher release angle.

days.guide: Record a slow-motion throw; compare each cue on video. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: On video, how can you tell hip rotation happened?
questions.a: The belly button turns from facing the side to facing the target before the arm comes through.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph using their data about how force and angle affected distance.

questions.q: If you throw with more force at the same angle, what happens?
questions.a: The ball travels farther.

weeks.assessment_key: Throwing data: distances for three angles and hits at three distances recorded. Written explanation (proficient): more force → farther; a middle angle (≈35–45°) went farthest; accuracy drops as distance increases; cites own numbers. 4 = all with data; 3 = most; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Gather a foam football or tennis ball and cones to mark routes. Review 'target hands': thumbs together for balls above the waist, pinkies together for balls below the waist. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Catching with stiff arms. Reach out and 'give' (pull the ball in toward the body) to absorb it.
Watching the thrower instead of the ball. Track the ball all the way into the hands.

days.guide: Toss balls high and low. Your child shows target hands: thumbs together above the waist, pinkies together below.

questions.q: How should your hands be for a ball below the waist?
questions.a: Pinkies together, fingers pointing down.

days.guide: Teach three routes with cones: slant (diagonal inward), out (straight then cut toward sideline), curl (run then turn back). Throw to your child on each route.

questions.q: Describe an 'out' route.
questions.a: Run straight downfield, then cut sharply toward the sideline.

days.guide: Your child catches on the run and immediately throws to a second target or person without extra steps.

questions.q: What helps you transition from catch to throw quickly?
questions.a: Catch with hands, bring the ball up to the throwing position right away, and step toward the new target.

days.guide: Play Ultimate ball: no running with the ball, pass to advance, score by catching in the end zone. Encourage passing to everyone.

questions.q: Why is a 'no running with the ball' rule good for including everyone?
questions.a: The team must pass to advance, so every player gets involved.

days.guide: Throw 10 passes to your child on the move and record catches. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: If you catch 7 of 10, what is your success rate?

weeks.assessment_key: Moving-catch success rate out of 10 recorded with percent. Cue check: target hands correct for high/low balls, eyes on the ball, gives with the catch, transitions to a throw. Proficient = 6/10 or better with 3 of 4 cues.

weeks.prep: Gather a flying disc (a 175 g Ultimate disc or a lighter kids' disc), hula hoops or cones for targets, and household objects to serve as 6 disc-golf 'holes.' Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Flinging with a big arm swing. The backhand is a short pull across the body ending in a wrist snap, which gives the disc spin.
Releasing the disc tilted. A tilted disc curves; keep it flat for a straight throw.

days.guide: Teach the backhand: thumb on top, fingers curled under the rim, side toward target, reach back across the body, step, and snap the wrist releasing the disc flat. Short 5 m throws.

questions.q: What makes a disc fly steadily?
questions.a: Spin from the wrist snap keeps it stable.

days.guide: Practice the pancake catch (one hand above, one below, clap together) and rim catches (thumb down for high, thumb up for low).

questions.q: Which catch is safest for beginners at chest height?
questions.a: The pancake (clap) catch.

days.guide: Throw through a hula hoop (held or hung) from 3, 5, 8 and 10 m. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Your throws keep curving left. What should you check?
questions.a: Whether the disc is tilted at release; keep it level and follow through toward the target.

days.guide: Set up 6 'holes' (trees, a bucket, a chair) and play a round, counting throws per hole. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: In disc golf, is a lower or higher score better?
questions.a: Lower — fewer throws to reach each target.

days.guide: Your child explains how the disc's angle affects flight and demonstrates a straight throw.

questions.q: What happens if the disc is tilted when released?
questions.a: It curves toward the side that is tipped down; a flat disc flies straight.

weeks.assessment_key: Disc golf scorecard: throws for each of 6 holes totaled correctly. Demonstration: flat release, step toward target, wrist snap, straight flight about 10 m (4 = consistent; 3 = mostly; 2 = sometimes; 1 = rarely). Explanation: a tilted disc curves toward the lower side.

weeks.prep: Gather a disc and cones for two end zones about 30–40 m apart. Read the basic Ultimate rules: no running with the disc, 10-second stall count, a dropped or intercepted pass changes possession, score by catching in the end zone. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Running with the disc. Once you catch, stop and pivot; you may only move your non-pivot foot.
Thinking 'spirit of the game' means no rules. Players follow the rules and call their own fouls honestly.

days.guide: Teach the pivot: keep one foot planted, step the other to fake and find an open lane. Practice faking then throwing.

questions.q: What is a pivot foot?
questions.a: The foot that stays planted after you catch the disc while the other foot steps to fake or throw.

days.guide: Explain modified rules and 'spirit of the game': players referee themselves, respect opponents and play fair.

questions.q: What happens if a pass is dropped?
questions.a: The other team gets the disc where it landed (turnover).

days.guide: Play a small-sided Ultimate game (2-v-2 or 3-v-3). Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: How do you get open for a pass?
questions.a: Cut quickly to empty space away from your defender and make eye contact with the thrower.

days.guide: Play with the rule that everyone must touch the disc before the team can score. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: How did the 'everyone touches' rule change how your team played?
questions.a: The team had to make more passes and include all players, so communication and teamwork increased.

days.guide: Skills test: 10 backhand throws to a partner at 10 m and 10 catches. Your child writes about spirit of the game.

questions.q: Give one example of spirit of the game.
questions.a: Calling your own foul, admitting a disc was out, or complimenting an opponent's play.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills test: throws caught by partner /10 and catches /10 (proficient ≈ 6+ each with correct backhand form). Reflection rubric: 4 = explains spirit of the game and gives two specific personal examples; 3 = one example; 2 = general; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Gather a basketball (size 6 or 5) or playground ball and cones. A smooth driveway or court works best. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Slapping the ball with the palm. Dribble with the finger pads, pushing the ball down.
Watching the ball. Keep eyes up and feel the ball with your fingertips.

days.guide: Do 1-minute drills: pound dribble, low dribble, crossover, around the leg. Cue: 'fingertips, waist high, eyes up.'

questions.q: Which part of the hand controls the dribble?
questions.a: The finger pads (fingertips), not the palm.

days.guide: Dribble through cones with the right hand, then the left, then crossing over at each cone.

questions.q: Which hand should you dribble with when a defender is on your right?
questions.a: Your left hand, keeping your body between the defender and the ball.

days.guide: On a whistle, switch between speed dribble (ball pushed out in front, higher bounce) and control dribble (low, close, body protecting).

questions.q: When would you use a control dribble?
questions.a: When a defender is close or you're in traffic.

days.guide: Your partner tries to tap the ball away; your child keeps the body and off-arm between the defender and the ball.

questions.q: How do you protect the ball while dribbling?
questions.a: Keep the ball low on the side away from the defender, with the body and off-arm (not pushing) as a shield.

days.guide: Time your child through the cone course using both hands. Record time and cue checklist. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Why practice with your weaker hand?
questions.a: So you can dribble away from defenders on either side.

weeks.assessment_key: Dribble course time recorded. Cue checklist: fingertips, ball at or below waist, eyes up, uses both hands, crossover at cones, keeps control. Proficient = 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Gather a basketball, a hoop (or a bucket/laundry basket target), and a wall. Learn BEEF: Balance, Eyes on target, Elbow under the ball, Follow-through ('reach into the cookie jar'). Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Shooting with two hands pushing. The shooting hand does the work; the other hand only guides.
Jumping off the wrong foot in a layup. A right-hand layup goes right foot, left foot, jump off the left and lift the right knee.

days.guide: Practice 20 chest passes (thumbs down on release), 20 bounce passes (bounce about 2/3 of the way to the target), 20 overhead passes against the wall.

questions.q: Where should a bounce pass hit the ground?
questions.a: About two-thirds of the way toward the receiver.

days.guide: Form shooting close to the basket using BEEF, 30 shots, one hand on the ball first. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What does BEEF stand for?
questions.a: Balance, Eyes, Elbow, Follow-through.

days.guide: Walk through right-hand layup footwork: step right, step left, jump off the left and lift the right knee, shoot off the backboard. Slowly first, then at speed.

questions.q: On a right-handed layup, which foot do you jump off?
questions.a: The left foot.

days.guide: Play Around the World at 5 spots; you must make a shot to move to the next spot. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What part of BEEF helps aim the ball?
questions.a: Eyes on the target and elbow pointing at the basket (under the ball).

days.guide: Video a few shots and check each BEEF cue; your child writes one fix to practice. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Your shot keeps falling short. Which cue might be missing?
questions.a: Balance/using the legs or a full follow-through—bend the knees and extend fully.

weeks.assessment_key: Self-assessment: for each BEEF cue mark yes/sometimes/no from video, plus one specific fix. Proficient = honest marks that match the video and a fix tied to a cue (e.g., 'snap my wrist and hold the follow-through').

weeks.prep: Gather a basketball and hoop. Draw a simple court diagram for Friday (paper or whiteboard). Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Crossing the feet on defense. Slide the feet without crossing so you can change direction quickly.
Standing still after passing. In a give-and-go, cut to the basket immediately after the pass.

days.guide: Teach the defensive stance: feet wide, knees bent, hands active, stay between the player and basket. Do 5 × 30-second slides.

questions.q: Why don't defenders cross their feet when sliding?
questions.a: Crossing makes you off-balance and slow to change direction.

days.guide: Teach the give-and-go: pass to a partner, cut toward the basket, get the ball back and finish with a layup.

questions.q: What does the 'go' mean in give-and-go?
questions.a: After giving (passing) the ball, you go (cut) toward the basket to get it back.

days.guide: Two attackers vs. you on defense: if you guard the ball carrier, they pass; if you stay back, they shoot or drive.

questions.q: In 2-v-1, when should the ball carrier pass?
questions.a: When the defender commits to them, leaving the teammate open.

days.guide: Play 2-v-2 half court; pause to point out open lanes and help defense. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What is help defense?
questions.a: Leaving your player slightly to stop a driving ball carrier, then recovering.

days.guide: Your child diagrams a give-and-go with arrows and explains it. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How does a give-and-go create an open lane?
questions.a: The defender turns to watch the pass, and the cutter moves quickly past them toward the basket into open space.

weeks.assessment_key: Strategy diagram: shows player A passing to B (dashed arrow), A cutting to the basket (solid arrow), B passing back, and A shooting; explanation mentions the defender watching the ball. Game observation: uses defensive stance, moves without the ball, passes to open teammates. Proficient = accurate diagram plus 2 of 3 game behaviors.

weeks.prep: Gather a basketball and hoop. Review the rules: traveling (moving pivot foot or walking without dribbling), double dribble (dribbling with two hands or dribbling again after stopping), fouls (illegal contact like pushing or hitting arms). Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Thinking any contact is a foul. Incidental contact is normal; a foul is illegal contact that gives an advantage (pushing, holding, hitting).
Arguing calls. Use respectful words and agreed methods to settle disputes.

days.guide: Act out traveling, double dribble and a foul; your child names each, then calls them fairly during play.

questions.q: You stop dribbling, then start dribbling again. What violation is that?
questions.a: Double dribble.

days.guide: Rotate through 3-minute stations (dribble, pass, shoot) then play 3-on-3 or 1-on-1. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Name two violations you watched for in the game.
questions.a: Any two: traveling, double dribble, fouls, out of bounds.

days.guide: Play with the rule that every player must receive a pass before a shot. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: How does the 'everyone receives a pass' rule help the team?
questions.a: It involves all players and builds passing and teamwork.

days.guide: Role-play three disputes (ball out of bounds? foul? who gets the ball?) and practice calm solutions: listen, state your view, agree on a fair fix (redo, rock-paper-scissors).

questions.q: What's a respectful way to settle a disputed call?
questions.a: Calmly explain what you saw, listen, then agree on a fair solution like a redo or rock-paper-scissors.

days.guide: Skills test: dribble the cone course, 10 passes to a target, 10 close shots. Your child completes a sportsmanship self-rating.

questions.q: What does fair play look like?
questions.a: Following rules, calling your own violations honestly, encouraging others, and respecting opponents and calls.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills test: dribble (both hands, control), passes (hits target 7+/10 proficient), shooting (BEEF form; makes 4+/10 close shots proficient). Sportsmanship self-rating 1–4 on: follows rules, honest calls, encourages others, accepts results; child gives one example for each.

weeks.prep: Find music: a Virginia Reel recording (fiddle tune) and a beginner line dance (e.g., Electric Slide-style). Learn the reel order from a short video. You need at least 2 couples—recruit family or play the extra role yourself. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Do-si-do and swing are the same. Do-si-do: pass right shoulders, go back-to-back, return without turning. Swing: link elbows (or hold) and turn around together.
Ignoring the music. Steps should land on the beat; listen for 8-count phrases.

days.guide: Teach do-si-do, promenade (side by side, walking counterclockwise holding hands), swing, and allemande left (left forearms, turn around and back).

questions.q: Describe a do-si-do.
questions.a: Partners walk forward, pass right shoulders, step back-to-back, then walk backward to place without turning.

days.guide: Teach the Virginia Reel figures in order: forward and back, right-hand turn, left-hand turn, two-hand turn, do-si-do, head couple sashays down and back, reel, cast off, arch. Connect it to colonial America.

questions.q: Where does the Virginia Reel come from?
questions.a: It's an Anglo-American country dance popular in colonial and early American times, related to English and Scottish reels.

days.guide: Teach grapevine (side, behind, side, touch), step-touch, and a quarter pivot turn; dance a simple line dance.

questions.q: What are the steps of a grapevine to the right?
questions.a: Step right, cross left behind, step right, touch left (or close).

days.guide: Take turns as caller, calling moves a few beats early so dancers move on the beat. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why does a caller call moves before the beat they start on?
questions.a: So dancers have time to hear it and begin the move right on the beat.

days.guide: Perform both dances for family. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Name two dance figures from this week.
questions.a: Any two: do-si-do, promenade, swing, allemande, sashay, grapevine, pivot turn.

weeks.assessment_key: Dance checklist (✓ each): performs figures in correct order, stays on the beat, knows partner/position, uses correct footwork for grapevine and pivot, shows courtesy to partners. Proficient = 4 of 5.

weeks.prep: Find music for La Raspa, the Hora (e.g., 'Hava Nagila'), and tinikling. For tinikling use two long poles, broom handles or two ropes on the ground. Read a short background for each dance before teaching. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Thinking folk dances are just steps. Each comes from a culture and often has meaning (celebration, imitating nature).
In tinikling, standing between the poles when they close. Hop out on the 'together' beat; poles stay low and moved gently.

days.guide: Teach La Raspa: the bleking (hop-step: hop and switch feet, heels forward) for 3 then a pause/clap, repeated; then the elbow-swing section with a partner.

questions.q: What country does La Raspa come from?
questions.a: Mexico.

days.guide: Teach the hora: circle with hands joined; basic step 'side, behind, side, kick, side, kick' moving around the circle.

questions.q: Where is the hora traditionally danced?
questions.a: It's a circle dance of Israel (and also danced in Romania and Jewish communities); it's common at celebrations like weddings.

days.guide: Teach tinikling: poles tapped twice apart, then brought together once (a 3-beat pattern). Practice the hop pattern beside ropes on the ground first, then with gentle moving poles.

questions.q: What does tinikling imitate?
questions.a: The tikling bird stepping between bamboo traps/grass stalks in the Philippines.

days.guide: Your child reads about each dance and shares one fact before dancing it. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Share one cultural fact about tinikling.
questions.a: Example: It is the national/folk dance of the Philippines and imitates the tikling bird dodging bamboo traps.

days.guide: Perform two dances; take pulse afterward. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Was your heart rate after dancing in an exercise range? What does that show?
questions.a: Usually yes (well above resting) — dancing is aerobic activity.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance (4 = correct steps and rhythm for two dances with no prompts; 3 = minor errors; 2 = needs frequent prompts; 1 = cannot perform). Cultural fact must be accurate: La Raspa—Mexico; Hora—Israel/Romania circle dance at celebrations; Tinikling—Philippines, imitates the tikling bird.

weeks.prep: Choose music with a clear beat (about 2 minutes). Have paper to write counts and a recording device. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Thinking canon and unison are the same. Unison = everyone does the same move at the same time; canon = the same move starts at different times, like a round.
Only using one level. Mix low (floor), middle and high levels for interest.

days.guide: Demonstrate levels (low, middle, high), formations (line, circle, diagonal), unison and canon with an 8-count phrase. Your child tries each.

questions.q: What is the difference between canon and unison?
questions.a: Unison: everyone moves the same at the same time. Canon: dancers start the same moves at different times, one after another.

days.guide: Plan 64 counts (eight 8-counts) on paper, noting moves, levels and formations. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: How many 8-count phrases are in 64 counts?
questions.a: Eight.

days.guide: Rehearse; fix timing and smooth transitions. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What is a transition in a dance?
questions.a: The movement that connects one section or move to the next.

days.guide: Record, watch, and revise one section. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What did you change and why?
questions.a: Answer varies; strong answers name a specific section and a reason (e.g., 'counts 17–24 were rushed, so I simplified the turn').

days.guide: Perform; your child explains how the dance uses rhythm and patterns. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: How does your dance show a pattern?
questions.a: Moves repeat or follow a structure in 8-count phrases (e.g., AB AB), timed to the beat.

weeks.assessment_key: Original dance rubric (1–4 each): 64 counts on beat; uses at least two levels, one formation change, and both unison and canon; smooth transitions; explanation of rhythm/pattern. Proficient = 3+ in each.

weeks.prep: Gather a beach ball or volleyball trainer (soft), and set a rope 'net' between two chairs about 1.5–2 m high. Review cues: ready position, flat platform, legs lift, no swing. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Swinging the arms. Hold a still platform and lift with the legs.
Hitting with the hands or fists. Contact the ball on the forearms above the wrists.

days.guide: Ready position: feet shoulder-width, knees bent, weight forward, arms out. Toss balls to the side; your child shuffles (no crossing feet) to get behind the ball.

questions.q: Why shuffle instead of run when moving to the ball?
questions.a: To stay square to the target and balanced in ready position.

days.guide: Make the platform: one hand in the other, thumbs together and pointing down, elbows locked. Self-bump a beach ball.

questions.q: Where on your arms should the ball hit?
questions.a: On the flat part of the forearms, between the wrists and elbows.

days.guide: Toss to your child; they bump back to you. Count consecutive good passes. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Your bump goes straight up behind you. What happened?
questions.a: The arms swung too high or the platform was angled up; keep the platform still and aimed at the target, lift with the legs.

days.guide: Toss at different heights; your child bumps to a hula hoop target. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: How do you aim a bump?
questions.a: Angle the platform toward the target and face it (square shoulders).

days.guide: Your child rates bump form on the three cues. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Name the three bump cues.
questions.a: Flat platform, legs lift, no swing.

weeks.assessment_key: Bump consecutive count recorded. Cue self-assessment (flat platform, legs lift, no swing, ready position) marked accurately. Proficient = 5+ consecutive bumps and 3 of 4 cues.

weeks.prep: Gather a beach ball or soft volleyball, rope net, and tape or cones to mark serve zones. Review 'triangle hands' (thumbs and index fingers form a triangle above the forehead). Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Slapping the set with palms. Contact with the finger pads, then extend arms and legs.
Tossing too high on the underhand serve. Hold the ball low and still, swing the other arm like a pendulum, hit the bottom of the ball.

days.guide: Teach the set: triangle hands above the forehead, contact with finger pads, extend arms and legs. Self-sets, then partner tosses.

questions.q: Where should your hands be when you set?
questions.a: Above the forehead in a triangle shape, using finger pads.

days.guide: Teach the underhand serve: opposite foot forward, hold ball at waist, swing the hitting arm back and through, contact the bottom of the ball with the heel of the hand. Start 3 m from the net, then move back.

questions.q: Which foot is forward for a right-handed underhand serve?
questions.a: The left foot.

days.guide: Rally over the net using bumps and sets; count your best cooperative rally. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: When do you set rather than bump?
questions.a: When the ball is high (above the forehead); bump low balls.

days.guide: Serve to marked zones; your child explains how force and contact point changed placement. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: If your serve goes into the net, what should you change?
questions.a: Use more force and/or contact slightly lower on the ball so it travels upward.

days.guide: Record serve success rate (out of 10) and best rally. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: If you made 7 of 10 serves, what percent is that?

weeks.assessment_key: Serve success rate /10 with correct percent; best rally count. Form: opposite foot forward, still ball, pendulum swing, heel of hand contact. Proficient = 5+/10 serves and a rally of 6+.

weeks.prep: Gather paddles (or paper plates taped to paint sticks), foam or wiffle balls, and tape a line on a wall about 1 m high. Set a low rope about 60 cm high for partner rallies. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Gripping like a frying pan. Use the 'shake hands' grip so you can hit both forehand and backhand.
Swinging hard. Control comes from a short, smooth swing and a firm wrist.

days.guide: Teach the shake-hands grip; bounce the ball up on the paddle 25 times. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What is the shake-hands grip?
questions.a: Hold the handle as if shaking hands, with the paddle face like an extension of the palm.

days.guide: Forehands against the wall above the line; count consecutive hits. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: For a forehand, which side of the body is the ball on?
questions.a: The same side as your hitting hand (palm-side).

days.guide: Backhands against the wall, then alternate forehand and backhand. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Which side of the paddle hits a backhand?
questions.a: The back-of-hand side, with the ball on the non-dominant side of the body.

days.guide: Rally with a partner over the low rope, soft control. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why use soft hits in a cooperative rally?
questions.a: Softer controlled hits are easier to return, so the rally lasts longer.

days.guide: Your child explains and demonstrates how paddle angle changes direction. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: If the paddle face is tilted up when you hit, where does the ball go?
questions.a: Upward/higher; tilted down sends it lower; angled sideways sends it that direction.

weeks.assessment_key: Wall-hit counts (forehand, backhand, alternating) recorded. Demonstration: open face → ball goes up, closed face → down, angled face → sideways in that direction. Proficient = 10+ consecutive forehands and correct explanation.

weeks.prep: Gather the rope net, beach ball, paddles and balls; chalk a four-square court (four squares about 2 × 2 m). Review the net skills checklist for Friday. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Hitting right back to the opponent. Aim for open space, away from the player.
Arguing line calls. Agree that the receiver calls their side honestly; when in doubt, replay.

days.guide: Play 1-v-1 paddle; points count only when the ball lands in open space. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Where should you aim to win points?
questions.a: Into open space, away from your opponent, especially deep or to the sides.

days.guide: Play 2-v-2 volleyball allowing one catch per side. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: How should two teammates share the court?
questions.a: Split responsibility (e.g., left/right or front/back) and call 'mine.'

days.guide: Play four square; review fair calls. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: In four square, what should you do on a close line call?
questions.a: Make an honest call; if unsure, replay the point.

days.guide: Discuss and write two strategies that won points. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Give one net-game strategy.
questions.a: Hit to open space; vary placement deep and short; return to ready position in the middle.

days.guide: Skills test: 10 bumps, 10 sets, 10 serves, 10 forehands; your child completes a fair-play self-check.

questions.q: What is a 'fair play' behavior in net games?
questions.a: Making honest calls, rotating fairly, encouraging others, shaking hands.

weeks.assessment_key: Net skills test, each out of 10: bump to target, set to target, underhand serve over net, forehand over the rope. Proficient = 5+/10 on each with correct cues. Fair-play self-check completed honestly with one example.

weeks.prep: Gather a plastic or foam bat, wiffle balls, and a tee (or a traffic cone). Mark a safe zone: no one stands within two bat lengths of the batter. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Choking the bat with knuckles misaligned. Line up the 'door-knocking' knuckles for a loose, quick swing.
Throwing the bat after hitting. Drop the bat before running.

days.guide: Teach the grip (dominant hand on top, knuckles aligned), athletic stance (feet shoulder-width, knees bent, side to the pitcher). Dry swings.

questions.q: For a right-handed batter, which hand is on top?
questions.a: The right hand.

days.guide: Hit 30 balls off a tee, aiming for line drives. Cue: swing level, eyes on the ball. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What is a line drive?
questions.a: A hit that travels fairly straight and low through the air, not high up or on the ground.

days.guide: Soft toss from the side (from a safe angle); your child tracks the ball to the bat. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Why watch the ball all the way to the bat?
questions.a: To time the swing and make solid contact.

days.guide: Review bat safety (safe zone, drop the bat, only swing in the batter's box) and play a target hitting game.

questions.q: After you hit the ball, what do you do with the bat?
questions.a: Drop it (not throw it) and run.

days.guide: Video a swing and check cues. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Name three batting cues.
questions.a: Knuckles aligned grip, side to the pitcher, step toward the pitcher, level swing, eyes on ball, follow through.

weeks.assessment_key: Batting cue checklist: grip knuckles aligned, balanced stance, small step toward pitcher, hips rotate, level swing, follow-through, drops bat safely. Proficient = 5 of 7.

weeks.prep: Gather a glove (or use bare hands with a soft ball), bases (cones or paper plates 30 ft/about 9 m apart), and soft balls. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Fielding grounders standing up. Get low, glove on the ground, 'alligator hands' (top hand covers).
Catching fly balls at the belly. Get under the ball and catch above the head with two hands.

days.guide: Roll 20 grounders; your child moves in front, gets low, glove down, top hand covers like an alligator's jaws.

questions.q: Why get in front of the ball?
questions.a: Your body acts as a backstop if the ball gets past the glove.

days.guide: Toss 20 fly balls; your child calls 'I got it,' gets under, catches above the head with two hands.

questions.q: Why call 'I got it'?
questions.a: So teammates know who is catching and nobody collides.

days.guide: Field and throw to a base 30 ft away; record accurate throws. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What should you do with your feet before throwing to a base?
questions.a: Step toward the base target with the opposite foot.

days.guide: Practice relay: outfielder throws to cutoff, cutoff turns and throws to a base. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Why use a cutoff throw?
questions.a: Two shorter, accurate throws are faster and more accurate than one long throw.

days.guide: Fielding test: 10 grounders and 10 flies. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What does 'alligator hands' mean?
questions.a: Glove open on the ground with the top hand above it ready to close over the ball.

weeks.assessment_key: Fielding test: grounders /10 and flies /10. Proficient = 7+ each with correct form (low, in front, two hands).

weeks.prep: Gather a playground ball and four bases (cones). Draw a diamond diagram for Friday. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Slowing down before first base. Run through first base; you can overrun it.
Running on a caught fly ball. Runners must tag up (return to their base) before advancing.

days.guide: Roll balls; your child kicks to left, center and right by turning the kicking foot and hips.

questions.q: To kick to the right side (for a right-footed kicker), what changes?
questions.a: Contact the ball later/with the inside of the foot angled right and point the hips toward right field.

days.guide: Practice running through first base, and rounding bases with a small curve. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Why can you run past first base?
questions.a: The rules allow overrunning first base, so you don't slow down.

days.guide: Explain force outs and tagging up; quiz with scenarios. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Runner on first, ball kicked on the ground. Where is the force out?
questions.a: At second base (and first for the kicker).

days.guide: Play a kickball game. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: If a fly ball is caught, what must runners do?
questions.a: Return to (tag) their base before advancing.

days.guide: Your child diagrams where to kick based on fielder positions. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: If all fielders are on the left side, where should you kick?
questions.a: To the right side/open space.

weeks.assessment_key: Kick placement: aims to left, center and right on request (proficient 2/3 each). Strategy diagram correctly places the kick in open space, explains why.

weeks.prep: Gather foam bat, wiffle balls, tee, and bases. Print a diagram of the 9 fielding positions. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Every fielder chases the ball. Each position covers an area and a base.
Thinking one strong player wins the game. Teamwork and positive talk matter.

days.guide: Play 'hit the bat and run' — batter hits, runs bases; fielders get the ball back to home. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What decides how many bases you can run?
questions.a: How quickly the fielders return the ball to home.

days.guide: Play a modified game off a tee, everyone bats each inning. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: How many outs in a half-inning?
questions.a: Three.

days.guide: Learn the 9 positions: pitcher, catcher, first base, second base, shortstop, third base, left field, center field, right field.

questions.q: Name the 9 fielding positions.
questions.a: Pitcher, catcher, first baseman, second baseman, shortstop, third baseman, left fielder, center fielder, right fielder.

days.guide: Play a full modified game; practice positive talk. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Give an example of positive teammate talk.
questions.a: 'Nice try! You'll get the next one.' or 'Great hustle!'

days.guide: Skills test (tee hits, grounders, flies); reflect on sportsmanship. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Why does sportsmanship matter in team games?
questions.a: It keeps the game fair, safe and fun, and builds trust among teammates and opponents.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills test: tee hits into fair territory /10, grounders /10, flies /10. Proficient = 6+ each. Reflection includes one specific example of good sportsmanship.

weeks.prep: Gather baseline FITNESSGRAM scores, a planning template (calendar), and an activity log. Know the FITT principle. Before each session: check the space for hazards, have water ready, wear athletic shoes, and stop if your child shows signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps).
misconceptions: Thinking more is always better. Increase gradually (overload) and include rest days.
Confusing type with intensity. Type = what activity; intensity = how hard.

days.guide: Explain FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type). Classify 10 activities (walking, sprinting, jump rope, yoga, push-ups, etc.).

questions.q: What does each letter of FITT stand for?
questions.a: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.

days.guide: Review baseline scores and choose two goals. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why base goals on your scores?
questions.a: Scores show which fitness areas need improvement.
